title: Data Contracts + Tool-Calling Workflow demo with SentinelAI
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-10 15:30 PT — duration ~52m; attendees listed above. Transcript auto-captured by Fireflies, medium fidelity.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is alex from Redwood Inference, i'm with priya (se) and raf (product). how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Jordan: good, thanks. excited to see the walkthrough — we've been rethinking our output validation for a few services.
[00:13] Priya: cool, quick agenda: 1) show JSON mode and schema contracts in the API, 2) demo tool/function calling with guardrails in the Console, 3) Optimize tips for cost/latency, and 4) Q&A + next steps.
[00:28] Marta: sounds good, we mainly care about strict schemas for clinical-note extraction pipelines — must be machine-parseable, deterministic fields, and tight error handling.
[00:37] Samir: and security — SOC2, KMS, audit logs; how the private deployment would handle payload retention.
[00:45] Alex: great, we'll touch those. i'll share my screen — showing the Redwood Console. quick note: some auto captions may say redwood "dedicaded" sometimes — ignore.
[01:05] [screen share begins] Priya: starting with the API explorer. here we set response_mode: json, and upload a JSON schema. you can pin a contract to a route so every response is validated.
[01:20] Jordan: when you say "pin a contract" is that per-model or per-route?
[01:24] Priya: per-route, route config overlays model selection. you can also set fallback policies if the model returns invalid JSON — like re-run with a stricter prompt or call a validator hook.
[01:37] Raf: showing an example schema for clinical_summary: fields like patient_id (string), summary_text (string, max 2k), diagnoses (array of codes), severity_score (number 0-100).
[01:50] Marta: do you support enums and pattern validation? we need ICD patterns.
[01:54] Priya: yes, full JSON Schema draft-07 style — we support regex patterns, enums, required, min/max, nested objects. there is a preview validator in the Console with quick failures.
[02:06] [02:06] Transcript note: occasional transcription errors; sometimes "K V cache" appears as "KV cash".
[02:12] Alex: switching to function/tool calling. we built a tool shim that can be attached to routes — think of it as a managed callback. you define a tool schema (inputs, auth token scope) and the runtime invokes the tool when the model requests it.
[02:29] Jordan: can that be used to retrieve patient metadata securely from our vault?
[02:33] Priya: yes — the tool can be executed in a VPC-backed private deploy, and you can restrict keys to a short-lived service account. Redwood Private lets you host the control plane in your VPC and uses your KMS for key wrapping.
[02:44] Samir: what about audit logs for each tool invocation? we need immutable traces for HIPAA audits.
[02:48] Raf: logs are exported to your S3 or GCS bucket with per-request metadata: route, model, tokens, tool-called, latency, and a hashed user id. you can set retention on the bucket side; we also offer an enterprise retention add-on.
[03:00] Tina: demo the actual function call flow please.
[03:03] Priya: ok, i'll trigger a live example. payload -> model -> model emits a function_call("get_patient_metadata", {patient_id: "1234"}) -> Redwood runtime intercepts -> validate function inputs -> call configured tool endpoint -> return result to model -> model composes final JSON.
[03:22] [03:22] Example live run: Model returned function_call with args; small delay ~400ms for the tool invocation.
[03:35] Jordan: is the validation done client-side or inside our private network?
[03:39] Priya: validation happens in the runtime — in Private, that's inside your network. for Hosted, validation is in Redwood's control plane but we only forward allowed fields; you can opt to run a validator webhook in your infra for max isolation.
[03:52] Alex: switching to the SDK; here's a Python snippet showing response_mode='json', schema_id='clinical_v2', and tool_calls enabled. the SDK will raise a StructuredOutputError if the response fails schema validation unless you set strict_mode=false.
[04:10] Marta: what default does strict_mode use? we want to fail fast.
[04:13] Priya: defaults to true on Dedicated and Private; hosted defaults to warn (non-blocking) to reduce user friction.
[04:22] Jordan: neat. about guardrails — how do you prevent hallucinated tool calls? we've seen models invent endpoints.
[04:29] Raf: the runtime requires registration of tool names and their input schemas. if the model asks for an unregistered tool, the runtime returns an error and optionally falls back to a safe-mode response. you can also set a denylist for specific output types.
[04:45] [04:45] Small cross-talk.
[04:50] Priya: demo: define tool with auth scope limited to GET /patients/{id}/meta, set rate limits, map role-based access so only service-account used by that route can call it.
[05:01] Samir: for encryption of payloads in transit and at rest?
[05:04] Alex: TLS for in-flight, envelope encryption at rest with your KMS, HSM integrations optional; we support customer-managed keys.
[05:13] Jordan: what about batching and KV cache for repeated patient prefix data? we want to reduce cost and latency for common reads.
[05:19] Priya: there's automatic prefix caching in the runtime; you can also declare cacheable keys for results returned by tool calls. cache TTLs, invalidation hooks are configurable. this reduces calls to downstream vaults.
[05:34] Marta: can we see the Optimize recommendations?
[05:36] Raf: switching to Redwood Optimize. it analyzes token distribution, latency histograms, and suggests quantization profiles and batching windows. it also simulates cost impact of switching a route from hosted to dedicated or using a 4-bit quantized variant.
[05:54] [05:54] Demo chart: token histogram peaked at ~350 tokens, suggests smaller batch sizes for sub-100ms p50 SLOs.
[06:05] Alex: note about fallbacks: you can configure multi-model routing by policy — primary high-quality model + cheaper quantized secondary; on capacity constraints runtime fails over seamlessly.
[06:18] Jordan: we have strict SLOs for 95th percentile under 200ms. can Redwood guarantee that on Dedicated?
[06:25] Priya: Dedicated with reserved GPUs and configured autoscale can meet that depending on model size and seq length; we provide performance profiles per model so you can size your pool. SLA add-on covers uptime and p95 latency targets.
[06:40] Tina: procurement question: what's the contract model for Dedicated vs Private?
[06:44] Alex: Dedicated is reserved capacity monthly commit; Private has platform licensing plus deployment support and an enterprise support tier. we sent a pricing snapshot last quarter — i'll re-share.
[06:55] Jordan: show me how you handle invalid JSON responses — example where model returns malformed array.
[07:01] Priya: live: model returned diagnoses: "diags": "N/A" instead of array; Console flagged it, ran validator, and we have an auto-remediate option: re-prompt with clarifying instruction or call a post-validator webhook.
[07:16] Marta: nice. can the post-validator webhook push a sanitized object back into the toolchain? we want to keep an audit of original and sanitized.
[07:23] Raf: yes, webhook receives original payload, returns the corrected document; both are stored in the audit log with deltas.
[07:33] [07:33] Transcription glitch: "audit log" captured as "odd it log" in one place.
[07:37] Alex: moving to integrations — common patterns: 1) direct SDK calls, 2) HTTP webhook for tool calls, 3) message queue fan-out for async jobs, 4) internal microservice adapter.
[07:52] Jordan: for our compliance team: SAML/SSO + SCIM provisioning?
[07:56] Priya: yes, SAML SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, RBAC with role templates, and audit hooks to push logs to your SIEM.
[08:06] Samir: what's the attack surface for tool endpoints?
[08:09] Raf: endpoints are secured with mTLS or bearer tokens; we recommend mTLS inside VPCs and short-lived tokens with trust boundaries.
[08:18] Tina: can we restrict what fields the model is allowed to output?
[08:21] Priya: through schema + output allowlist/denylist. you can also redact sensitive fields in a post-processing policy before storing.
[08:30] Jordan: how do you handle model updates/rollouts without breaking contracts?
[08:34] Alex: model pinning — routes can pin to exact model version. for rollouts we support canaries and A/B tests with automatic rollback if schema fail rates increase or quality regressions are detected by evals tied to your prompt sets.
[08:51] [08:51] Example canary run UI where % traffic is routed.
[09:00] Marta: do we get token-level cost breakdowns by route?
[09:04] Raf: yes, the Console shows token counts, embeddings, tool call egress, and an estimated cost per response — delta by model variant is visible.
[09:15] Jordan: any limitations on schema complexity? deep nested objects?
[09:19] Priya: we support nested objects and arrays, but very deep recursion could hit validation timeouts; we recommend flattening or chunking very large payloads.
[09:31] Samir: about data residency — can Private be deployed in our on-prem racks?
[09:35] Alex: yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped or regulated environments with a private control plane and local metric sinks.
[09:44] [09:44] Audience question: will function calls be visible in audit stream?
[09:46] Priya: yes — tool invocation metadata is included, you can include request/response bodies or just metadata depending on retention settings.
[09:54] Jordan: okay, let's talk failure modes: network outage during tool call — runtime behavior?
[09:59] Raf: configurable: retry policy, fail-fast, or degrade to cached response. you can set a fallback policy to return a partial JSON with nulls and an errors array.
[10:12] Marta: can we get an example of the SDK raising StructuredOutputError and how to handle it?
[10:17] Alex: here's a code example: try: response = client.generate(...), except StructuredOutputError as e: log(e.schema_errors); call remediation pipeline. you can also set on_error: forward_to_human_review.
[10:33] Tina: how do you inspect per-token latency?
[10:36] Raf: trace view — shows model generation timeline, kernel time, kv cache hits, and tool call time. you can drill into a single request and see timestamps.
[10:48] [10:48] Short break while Alex pulls a benchmark spreadsheet.
[11:05] [11:05] Benchmark: p50 85ms, p95 210ms for a 6B model on Dedicated with certain batching.
[11:18] Jordan: we need a POC to validate SLOs and the tool-calling flow with our vault. timeline: 6 week pilot.
[11:25] Alex: good — typical POC steps: 1) access to sandbox + test route, 2) share sample prompt set and schema, 3) run bench tests, 4) security review. we can start next week.
[11:35] Samir: we'll need an inventory of all data flows and a SOC2 questionnaire.
[11:40] Priya: i'll attach the security pack and SOC2 artifacts. Alex will send the POC checklist and sandbox creds.
[11:48] Jordan: any competitors we should be aware of?
[11:51] Alex: you might see Anthropic for safety tooling, OpenAI for hosted simplicity, and Cohere for embeddings — each has tradeoffs.
[11:59] Tina: cost question: is there a breakout for tool call egress or is it bundled?
[12:03] Raf: tool call egress is shown as separate line items in the cost view.
[12:10] [12:10] Q&A winds down.
[12:12] Priya: recap: we demonstrated JSON mode + schema validation, function/tool-calling with guarded registries, Optimize recommendations, and audit/retention controls.
[12:22] Alex: next steps: we'll provision a sandbox, share security docs, and propose a POC scope & price.
[12:28] Jordan: thanks, this was helpful. we'll follow up with a list of schemas and sample clinical prompts.
[12:33] [end of recording]

Share POC scope and pricing (Alex Morgan)
Customer to deliver sample prompt set and schemas (Jordan Lee)
